title: Expected breaker failures, year by year

blocks.text: A transmission company runs a fleet of circuit breakers of one type, with Weibull shape `beta` and scale `eta` (years). A failed breaker is repaired and put back without being made any younger, so it can fail again. The maintenance shop sizes its spares from the fleet's expected failures in each of the coming years.

items: `failures_by_year(ages, beta, eta, years)`: a list of `years` numbers, the whole fleet's expected failures in the coming year, the year after, and so on; `ages` are the breakers' ages today;
`chance_of_none(age, beta, eta, years)`: the chance that one breaker, working today at `age`, has no failure at all in the next `years` years.

blocks.text: Write both in the lesson's notation first, with $`\Lambda(t) = (t/\eta)^\beta`$. The tests compare with `scipy.stats.weibull_min.logsf`, whose negative is $`\Lambda`$. About seven lines.

ages = [5, 18, 33]

print("ages 5, 18, 33 over 4 years:", [round(v, 4) for v in failures_by_year(ages, 3.0, 40.0, 4)])
print("one new breaker, first year:", [round(v, 6) for v in failures_by_year([0], 3.0, 40.0, 1)])
print("no failure for age 33 in 3 years:", round(chance_of_none(33, 3.0, 40.0, 3), 4))
print("no failure for age 5 in 3 years:", round(chance_of_none(5, 3.0, 40.0, 3), 4))

cases.says: a single new breaker's expected failures in its first year is its cumulative hazard at age 1
every breaker is one year older in each later year
a repaired breaker can fail more than once a year, so the expected count can exceed one per breaker
the chance of no failure is that of a breaker working today

origin.section: Count Expected Failures When a Failed Asset Is Repaired and Kept

concepts: under minimal repair the expected count of failures is the growth of the cumulative hazard
